paragraphs.text: וְיָצָ֥א חֹ֖טֶר מִגֵּ֣זַע יִשָׁ֑י וְנֵ֖צֶר מִשָּׁרָשָׁ֥יו יִפְרֶֽה׃ וְנָחָ֥ה עָלָ֖יו ר֣וּחַ יְהוָ֑ה ר֧וּחַ חָכְמָ֣ה וּבִינָ֗ה ר֤וּחַ עֵצָה֙ וּגְבוּרָ֔ה ר֥וּחַ דַּ֖עַת וְיִרְאַ֥ת יְהוָֽה׃ וַהֲרִיחֹ֖ו בְּיִרְאַ֣ת יְהוָ֑ה וְלֹֽא־לְמַרְאֵ֤ה עֵינָיו֙ יִשְׁפֹּ֔וט וְלֹֽא־לְמִשְׁמַ֥ע אָזְנָ֖יו יֹוכִֽיחַ׃ וְשָׁפַ֤ט בְּצֶ֙דֶק֙ דַּלִּ֔ים וְהֹוכִ֥יחַ בְּמִישֹׁ֖ור לְעַנְוֵי־אָ֑רֶץ וְהִֽכָּה־אֶ֙רֶץ֙ בְּשֵׁ֣בֶט פִּ֔יו וּבְר֥וּחַ שְׂפָתָ֖יו יָמִ֥ית רָשָֽׁע׃ וְהָ֥יָה צֶ֖דֶק אֵזֹ֣ור מָתְנָ֑יו וְהָאֱמוּנָ֖ה אֵזֹ֥ור חֲלָצָֽיו׃ וְגָ֤ר זְאֵב֙ עִם־כֶּ֔בֶשׂ וְנָמֵ֖ר עִם־גְּדִ֣י יִרְבָּ֑ץ וְעֵ֨גֶל וּכְפִ֤יר וּמְרִיא֙ יַחְדָּ֔ו וְנַ֥עַר קָטֹ֖ן נֹהֵ֥ג בָּֽם׃ וּפָרָ֤ה וָדֹב֙ תִּרְעֶ֔ינָה יַחְדָּ֖ו יִרְבְּצ֣וּ יַלְדֵיהֶ֑ן וְאַרְיֵ֖ה כַּבָּקָ֥ר יֹֽאכַל־תֶּֽבֶן׃ וְשִֽׁעֲשַׁ֥ע יֹונֵ֖ק עַל־חֻ֣ר פָּ֑תֶן וְעַל֙ מְאוּרַ֣ת צִפְעֹונִ֔י גָּמ֖וּל יָדֹ֥ו הָדָֽה׃ לֹֽא־יָרֵ֥עוּ וְלֹֽא־יַשְׁחִ֖יתוּ בְּכָל־הַ֣ר קָדְשִׁ֑י כִּֽי־מָלְאָ֣ה הָאָ֗רֶץ דֵּעָה֙ אֶת־יְהוָ֔ה כַּמַּ֖יִם לַיָּ֥ם מְכַסִּֽים׃ פ

1 ويخرج قضيب من جذع يسى وينبت غصن من أصوله 2 ويحل عليه روح الرب روح الحكمة والفهم روح المشورة والقوة روح المعرفة ومخافة الرب . 3 ولذته تكون في مخافة الرب فلا يقضي بحسب نظر عينيه ولا يحكم بحسب سمع أذنيه . 4 بل يقضي بالعدل للمساكين ويحكم بالإنصاف لبائسي الأرض ويضرب الأرض بقضيب فمه ويميت المنافق بنفخة شفتيه . 5 ويكون البر منطقة متنيه والأمانة منطقة حقويه 6 فيسكن الذئب مع الخروف ويربض النمر مع الجدي والعجل والشبل والمسمن معا وصبي صغير يسوقها . 7 والبقرة والدبة ترعيان . تربض أولادهما معا والأسد كالبقر يأكل تبنا . 8 ويلعب الرضيع على سرب الصل ويمد الفطيم يده على حجر الأفعوان . 9 لا يسوؤون ولا يفسدون في كل جبل قدسي لأن الأرض تمتلئ من معرفة الرب كما تغطي المياه البحر

"And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots: And the spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the LORD; And shall make him of quick understanding in the fear of the LORD: and he shall not judge after the sight of his eyes, neither reprove after the hearing of his ears: But with righteousness shall he judge the poor, and reprove with equity for the meek of the earth: and he shall smite the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips shall he slay the wicked. And righteousness shall be the girdle of his loins, and faithfulness the girdle of his reins.

The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; and the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; and a little child shall lead them. And the cow and the bear shall feed; their young ones shall lie down together: and the lion shall eat straw like the ox. And the sucking child shall play on the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the cockatrice' den.
They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain: for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea."

"A Psalm for Solomon. Give the king thy judgments, O God, and thy righteousness unto the king's son. He shall judge thy people with righteousness, and thy poor with judgment. The mountains shall bring peace to the people, and the little hills, by righteousness. He shall judge the poor of the people, he shall save the children of the needy, and shall break in pieces the oppressor. quote_layout_review.caption: Abu Sa'id's report, Ibn al-Munadi, al-Malahim, p. 188

paragraphs.text: الحسن ، عن العلاء بن بشير (1) ، عن أبي الصديق الناجي ، عن أبي سعيد الخدري ، عن النبيّ ﵌ أنّه قال : أبشروا بالمهدي ، رجل من عترتي ، يخرج في اختلاف من الناس وزلازل ، فيملأ الأرض قسطا وعدلا ، كما ملئت جورا وظلما ، ويرضى عنه ساكن السماء ، وساكن الأرض ، ويقسم المال صحاحا (2) . قالوا : وما صحاحا ؟ قالوا : بالسويّة ، ويملأ اللّه قلوب امّة محمّد ﵌ غناء ، ويسعهم عدله ، حتّى أنّه ليأمر مناديه فينادي : من له إلى مال حاجة ؟ فما يأتيه أحد ، إلّا رجل واحد ، يأتيه فيسأله ، فيقول له : انطلق إلى السادن ، حتّى يعطيك . قال : فيأتيه فيقول له : أنا رسول المهديّ ، لتعطيني مالا ، فيقول له : احث (3) ، فيحثي فلا يستطيع أن يحمله ، فيلقي حتّى يكون قدر ما يستطيع حمله ، فيخرج به ، فيندم . فيقول : إذا ، كنت أجشع امّة محمّد نفسا ، دعتني إلى هذا المال ، وقد تركه غيري ، قال : فيرجع ، فيردّه عليه ، فيقول له : هذا المال لا نقبل منه شيئا ، اعطيناكه . قال : فيلبث بذلك سبعا ، [ أو ] ثمانيا ، [ أو ] تسع سنين (4) ، كذلك لا خير في الحياة بعده (5) .

Al-Hasan, from al-Ala ibn Bashir (1), from Abu al-Siddiq al-Naji, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet, who said, "Receive glad tidings of the Mahdi, a man from my progeny. He will emerge amid disagreement among people and earthquakes. He will fill the earth with equity and justice as it has been filled with injustice and oppression. The inhabitant of heaven and the inhabitant of earth will be pleased with him, and he will distribute wealth in full portions (2)."

They said, "What does 'in full portions' mean?" He said, "Equally." God will fill the hearts of Muhammad's community with sufficiency, and his justice will encompass them, so much so that he will order his caller to proclaim, "Who has need of wealth?" No one will come to him except one man. He will come and ask him, and he will say to him, "Go to the keeper, so that he may give you."

He said, "He will go to him and say, 'I am the Mahdi's messenger, so give me wealth.' He will say to him, 'Take a handful' (3). He will take a handful, but will not be able to carry it. So he will put back enough that he can carry, then leave with it and regret it. He will say, 'Then I am the most covetous soul in Muhammad's community. This wealth called me, while others left it.' He will return and give it back to him, but he will say, 'We do not accept anything back from this wealth. We gave it to you.'"
He will remain thus for seven, or eight, or nine years (4). There is no good in life after him (5).

The job-description metaphor obscures the interpretive claim and its limits. Original: summary: Revelation's woman, Ishmael's twelve princes, and the Bible's reigning king of justice converge, by job description rather than by name, on Fatimah, the twelve Imams, and the Mahdi. Applied correction: summary: Imami reports associate the sun and moon with Muhammad and Ali, count twelve Imams, and describe the Mahdi as a ruler of justice. Later writers use these reports to interpret Revelation 12 and other biblical passages.

Later books inaccurately groups Genesis with Revelation, and without naming anyone is too broad. The source locations are useful. Original: > 1. The Bible's later books describe, without naming anyone, a woman whose sign is a sun, a moon, and a crown of twelve stars (Revelation 12:1), twelve princes from Ishmael (Genesis 17:20), and a future king who judges the poor and fills the earth with justice and the knowledge of God (Isaiah 11:1-9, Psalm 72, Daniel 7:13-14). Applied correction: > 1. Revelation 12:1 describes a woman clothed with the sun, with the moon beneath her feet and a crown of twelve stars. Genesis 17:20 promises Ishmael twelve princes. Isaiah 11:1-9, Psalm 72, and Daniel 7:13-14 describe righteous rule and dominion.

This sentence needs two sentences and clear Imami/Sunni distinctions. Original: > 3. Shia and Sunni collections report twelve successors from Quraysh, the Musnad of Ahmad ties the number to the twelve chiefs of the Children of Israel, and the Imami reports name twelve Imams, first Ali קּ and last the Mahdi, eleven of them Fatimah's כֿ descendants. The heading starts with a defensive denial rather than the subject. Original: ## No verse names the house Applied correction: ## Biblical images and the Prophet's family

The third sentence repeats the first and narrates the case. Universal no verse should be scoped to the cited passages. Original: No verse of the Hebrew Bible or the New Testament names Muhammad ﷺ, Ali ﵇, Fatimah ﵍, or any Imam. Christians who expect a coming king read the same books and find Jesus ﵇ in them. A claim that the Bible contains the Prophet's family by name would be false, and the case made here does not rest on one. Their identification with these figures depends on parallels with the descriptions of the Prophet's family in Islamic reports.

The Bible inventory repeats the abstract, and the question adds no uncertainty beyond the qualification just stated. Original: What the Bible does contain is a set of unnamed figures defined by relations and by work. A woman stands clothed with the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars (Revelation 12:1). Ishmael is promised twelve princes and a great nation (Genesis 17:20). A future king from Jesse judges the poor with righteousness, kills the wicked, and fills the earth with the knowledge of God (Isaiah 11:1-9). The question here is narrow. Do the job descriptions the Bible assigns to its unnamed figures match the assignments the Islamic corpus itself makes, in its own reports, to the Prophet's house? Applied correction:

Without forcing a single verse certifies fairness. The rest recaps the abstract with a hypothetical that becomes a conclusion without accounting for mismatches. Original: That question can be answered without forcing a single verse. The Qur'an swears by a sun and a moon, and the Imams' transmitted exegesis names that sun and that moon. The Prophet ﷺ is reported in Shia and Sunni collections alike to have counted twelve successors and to have tied that number to the twelve chiefs of the Children of Israel. He is reported to have described an end-time ruler from Fatimah's ﵍ descendants who fills the earth with justice, and to have distinguished that ruler from the returning Isa ﵇. If those reports carry the Tradition's own assignment of the sky's lights to the Prophet's house, and its own count of twelve, then the Bible's woman, its twelve princes, and its reigning king describe a configuration the Islamic sources had already assembled under names. Applied correction:

A reading can be weighed has no content. The Christian alternative needs an actual source and a specific description later. The heading and callout locator already identify Revelation12 and its sign. Original: The twelfth chapter of Revelation begins with a sign in heaven. Applied correction:

The war moves hides the dragon's action. This short paraphrase is useful with quotations collapsed. Original: Her child is caught up to God, and the war moves to the rest of her seed. Applied correction: The woman's child is taken to God and his throne. The dragon then attacks her remaining offspring, who keep God's commandments and bear witness to Jesus.

Keep only the added identity from Revelation12:9. The quoted passages already state the crown and child's rule. Original: Three elements define the woman. She is associated with the sun, with the moon, and with exactly twelve stars. The dragon is identified within the chapter itself as Satan (Revelation 12:9), and the male child is the one destined to rule the nations. The passage does not name the woman, and readers have supplied the name for two thousand years. Applied correction: Revelation 12:9 identifies the dragon as Satan.

Never settled is too sweeping; states in one line adds nothing; the quoted verse places the sun around the woman, not under her feet. Preserve exact inline quotations. Original: Christian interpretation has never settled on one woman. Pope Pius XII, defining the Assumption of Mary in 1950, wrote that the scholastic doctors recognized the Assumption as signified in "that woman clothed with the sun whom John the Apostle contemplated on the Island of Patmos" (Munificentissimus Deus 27). The Catholic Encyclopedia's article on the Apocalypse states the historical-critical reading in one line. "The woman in travail is a personification of the synagogue or the church. Her first-born is Christ, her other seed is the community of the faithful" (Van den Biesen, "Apocalypse," 1907). The same article reads the imagery through Israel's own scriptures, noting the crown of twelve stars and the sun and moon under her feet with a cross-reference to Genesis 37:9-10, Joseph's dream. Applied correction: Pope Pius XII, defining the Assumption of Mary in 1950, wrote that the scholastic doctors recognized the Assumption as signified in "that woman clothed with the sun whom John the Apostle contemplated on the Island of Patmos" (Munificentissimus Deus 27). The Catholic Encyclopedia gives another interpretation: "The woman in travail is a personification of the synagogue or the church. Her first-born is Christ, her other seed is the community of the faithful" (Van den Biesen, "Apocalypse," 1907). The same article connects the sun, moon, and twelve stars with Joseph's dream in Genesis 37:9-10.

The chapter still asks for her is theatrical. None is a fact and any reading names a household dismiss alternatives without argument. Preserve the specific Genesis comparison. Original: The standard Christian identifications are Mary, the Church, and Israel, and the encyclopedia's own cross-reference sends the image back to Joseph's dream, in which the sun and the moon and eleven stars bow to one of Jacob's sons (Genesis 37:9). On the Israel reading the woman is Jacob's household and the sign retells the dream. That explains where the image came from. It does not settle who the woman is, and the chapter's war between her seed and the dragon still asks for her. None of these readings is a fact about the text. Each is an assignment, and the assignment has to fit the figure's relations. A woman whose sign is a sun she wears, a moon under her feet, and twelve stars as her crown is a woman set among those lights, and any reading of her names a household for them. Applied correction: In Joseph's dream, the sun, moon, and eleven stars bow to him (Genesis 37:9-10). This supplies a biblical parallel for Revelation's imagery, although Revelation has twelve stars and depicts a woman with a child.
Heading and source callout already say this. Original: The Qur'an opens the ninety-first sura with an oath. Applied correction:

Tala is the verb in the moon clause, not the verb by which the oath is made; reading of the school implies unanimity contradicted below. Original: The verb of the oath is tala, to follow. Ali ibn Ibrahim al-Qummi records the reading of the school with a full chain. Applied correction: In the moon clause, tala means “to follow.” Al-Qummi transmits Abu Basir's report of al-Sadiq's interpretation.

First four sentences repeat the translation as authorial fact. A concise comparison can preserve the meaningful difference between the reports. Original: The sun is Muhammad ﷺ, through whom God made the religion clear. The moon that follows him is Ali ﵇. The night that covers is the seizure of rule from the family of the Messenger ﷺ. The day that reveals is an Imam from Fatimah's ﵍ descendants who answers questions about the Prophet's religion. Furat ibn Ibrahim al-Kufi, who died in the fourth century, carries the same distribution from al-Husayn ﵇ himself. Applied correction: In the report transmitted by al-Qummi, al-Sadiq identifies the sun with Muhammad ﷺ and the moon with Ali ﵇. The day represents an Imam from Fatimah's descendants who explains the Prophet's religion. Furat transmits a report attributed to al-Husayn that identifies the day specifically with the Qa'im, the Imam who will fill the earth with justice.

The answer is yes and not a single stray voice add no evidence. Independent chains is a source judgment to verify. Original: The answer to the opening question is yes. In the Imami transmission the sun of the oath is the Prophet ﷺ and its moon is Ali ﵇, and the day is the Qa'im, the one who rises, who fills the earth with justice. The reading is not a single stray voice. Al-Kulayni's al-Kafi carries it in the Rawda volume, and al-Qummi and Furat carry it through independent chains, with Ibn Abbas versions beside them in Furat and Ibn Shahrashub. One recorded variant assigns the figures differently. Applied correction: Al-Kafi also transmits the sun-and-moon interpretation in its Rawda volume. Furat preserves versions attributed to Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Shahrashub includes related interpretations attributed to al-Baqir and al-Sadiq. Ta'wil al-Ayat preserves a different interpretation.

Final sentence says what Revelation would need, leaking research strategy. Preserve the alternate assignment and dependence among sources. Original: In this version the sun is Ali ﵇, the moon is al-Hasan and al-Husayn ﵈, and the heaven is Muhammad ﷺ. Sharaf al-Din al-Astarabadi, who collected it in Ta'wil al-Ayat, transmits it through two chains that converge on one report, the line of Abu Jamila from al-Halabi beside the line of Ali ibn al-Hakam, and al-Burhan and Bihar al-Anwar carry it from him rather than independently. The version that makes the sun the Prophet ﷺ and the moon Ali ﵇ is the one with the wider distribution in the early collections, in al-Kafi, al-Qummi, Furat, and Ibn Shahrashub's Manaqib. In the early transmission of the school, that is the reading of the oath the woman of Revelation 12 would need. Applied correction: In this version, the sun is Ali ﵇, the moon represents al-Hasan and al-Husayn ﵈, and the heaven is Muhammad ﷺ. Al-Astarabadi transmits it through two chains in Ta'wil al-Ayat. Al-Burhan and Bihar al-Anwar reproduce his report. The identification of the sun with Muhammad and the moon with Ali also appears in al-Kafi, al-Qummi, Furat, and Ibn Shahrashub's Manaqib.

Reports do not leave pair is source-as-performance narration. Three chains requires checking because two are printed. Original: The reports do not leave the sun and the moon as a pair. Al-Saduq devotes a chapter of Ma'ani al-Akhbar to the question and gathers three chains to one report. Applied correction: A report in al-Saduq's Ma'ani al-Akhbar associates Venus with Fatimah and the two Farqads with Hasan and Husayn.

Not Shia property alone stages a concession. Keep identified transmitters and their dependence. Original: The five lights of the sky are the five of the house, and the report is not Shia property alone. Al-Safuri al-Shafi'i carries it in Nuzhat al-Majalis and names his source, al-Thalabi's Ara'is, and al-Natanzi carries it in al-Khasais. Applied correction: Al-Safuri includes the report in Nuzhat al-Majalis, citing Ara'is. Ibn Shahrashub also attributes it to al-Natanzi's al-Khasa'is.

Extends constellation sounds like al-Khazzaz composed the mapping. Original: Al-Khazzaz al-Qummi extends the constellation to the full twelve, in the report of Salman. Applied correction: In Salman's report, transmitted by al-Khazzaz, the shining stars are nine Imams descended from al-Husayn.

The paragraph states the mapping twice and disguises the star-count mismatch. Keep actual comparison and exact limitation. Original: The shining stars are the nine Imams from al-Husayn's ﵇ loins, the ninth their Mahdi, and the count is tied, in the Prophet's ﷺ own words as reported, to the twelve tribes of Yaqub and the twelve apostles of Isa ﵇. Count the figures. Revelation places a woman, a sun, a moon, and twelve stars in one sign. The code places the sun, the moon, Venus, and the two Farqads over the Prophet ﷺ, Ali ﵇, Fatimah ﵍, al-Hasan ﵇, and al-Husayn ﵇, and the shining stars over the nine Imams after al-Husayn ﵇. No report assigns the crown itself. The reports give the moon to Ali, the two Farqads to al-Hasan and al-Husayn, and nine shining stars to the Imams after al-Husayn, while the Tablet family of reports counts the Imams as twelve. Reading Revelation's crown of twelve as those twelve Imams, with Ali among them beside his moon, is where the inference begins. Applied correction: Salman's report lists twelve successors and compares their number with Jacob's tribes and Jesus's apostles. Its celestial images distinguish Ali as the moon, Hasan and Husayn as the two Farqads, and nine later Imams as shining stars. Revelation instead gives the woman a crown of twelve stars. Identifying that crown with all twelve Imams therefore assigns Ali a place among the stars as well as the moon. The quoted Islamic reports do not make that identification.

One qualification belongs here is empty. No classical support exceeds a located report. Original: One qualification belongs here, because the obvious bridge from Joseph's dream to the Imams has no classical support. The Imam-side tafsirs of Qur'an 12:4 read Joseph's dream literally. Applied correction: Al-Qummi's report from al-Baqir interprets Joseph's dream through Joseph's own family.

Names even listed sneers without reason. Known to this corpus is research narration, and inference qualification repeats line212. No classical Imam-side exegesis of 12:4 known to this corpus reads the dream as the Prophet's ﵇ house. The assignments of the sky's lights above stand on their own reports. Reading Revelation 12 through them is an inference of the argument, not a transmitted interpretation. Applied correction: The sun represents Joseph's mother, the moon Jacob, and the eleven stars his brothers.

Complete mapping overclaims; strains arithmetic is indirect. Exhibit keeps text narrates editing. Original: The mapping is complete, woman, sun, moon, crown, and the encyclopedia's phrase about the sons strains the arithmetic by one, since eleven of the twelve descend from her and the count includes her husband. The full form, with the dragon and the child, appears in the earliest Imami carrier found, Ilzam al-Nasib of al-Yazdi al-Ha'iri, written in the early fourteenth century AH. His rendering of the vision paraphrases loosely and folds in clauses about mountains lowered and rough places smoothed that Revelation itself does not carry; the exhibit keeps his text as it stands. The Imami sequence quoted here contains eleven of her descendants and her husband, Ali, so his wording does not match that count. Al-Yazdi al-Ha'iri gives a longer interpretation in Ilzam al-Nasib. His paraphrase includes mountains being lowered and rough places made smooth, clauses absent from Revelation 12.

Retain attributions and separate alternatives; do not adopt al-Ha'iri's Jesus inference. Original: Al-Ha'iri reads the dragon as the tree of Banu Umayyah, the male child as the hidden Qa'im, and the iron rod as his sword, and he argues that the child cannot be Jesus ﵇ because Jesus ﵇ never fought. He records the Christian exegesis of his own day, which read the woman as the temple or the church, and rejects it, and he offers an alternative distribution of his own in which the twelve stars are Muhammad ﷺ, Ali ﵇, and ten of his descendants and the moon is the Qa'im. Applied correction: Al-Ha'iri identifies the dragon with Banu Umayyah, the child with the hidden Qa'im, and the iron rod with his sword. He rejects the identification of the child with Jesus on the ground that Jesus never fought. He also proposes a different mapping: Muhammad, Ali, and ten descendants form the twelve stars, and the Qa'im is the moon.

The paragraph mixes search logs, unsupported frequency judgments, and genuine provenance. Keep earliest located source explicitly qualified, name variants only after supplying citations. Original: The provenance has a limit that matters. A corpus search for the woman of Revelation 12 across the classical Imami literature, al-Kafi, the tafsirs, Bihar al-Anwar in its hundred and more volumes, returns nothing before the modern period. The earliest explicit carrier found is Ilzam al-Nasib. The argumentative ancestry runs through Jawad ibn Ibrahim Sabat al-Hanafi, whose Revelation material later Imami authors recycled, and Milani's Nafahat al-Azhar carries that line in its eighteenth volume. The modern authors also disagree with one another. One makes the sun Ali ﵇ and the woman's travail her miscarriage of Muhsin, and one makes the woman Narjis, the Mahdi's mother, with the sun as Imam al-Hasan al-Askari ﵇. The reading of the woman as Fatimah ﵍, with her father as the sun and her husband as the moon, is the commonest modern form, and Mawsu'at Karbala states it in its cleanest shape. (The encyclopedia's chapter reference slips by one. The quotation is Revelation 12:1.) Applied correction: Baydun cites chapter 11 for a quotation from Revelation 12:1.

Never reads makes a corpus search universal. Exactly those signs contradicts line212. Inference already preserved. Original: The classical Imami corpus never reads Revelation 12, and the reading of it as Fatimah ﵍ is modern. The modern reading assembles elements the classical corpus had already transmitted, the sun as the Prophet ﷺ and the moon as Ali ﵇ in the exegesis of Qur'an 91, the nine shining stars as the Imams from al-Husayn's line in the Salman report, and the woman as the one whose father, husband, and descendants they are. The Bible supplies a sign whose elements are a sun, a moon, and twelve stars around one woman. The Islamic corpus supplies a house whose members carry exactly those signs. The connection between the two is a modern inference, and it stands here as one. Applied correction:
Chronology of books adds no reasoning here. Original: The numerical promise is older than Revelation. Applied correction:

Al-Nu'mani records an interpretation connecting Ishmael's twelve princes with twelve Imams.

Treats the scholar's claimed Torah text as actual Torah evidence. The translation already supplies dictation details. Al-Rawandi's Kharaij carries the Torah quotation with the gloss attached. Applied correction: Al-Rawandi also relates the blessing of Ishmael to Muhammad ﷺ.

Majlisi, in the seventeenth century, records that he heard the Hebrew text from People of the Book he trusted. Applied correction: Majlisi, writing in the seventeenth century, says he heard the Hebrew passage read and translated by People of the Book whom he trusted.

Received text and doubled word may disguise a linguistic claim; preserve attribution, do not authenticate Hebrew. Original: Majlisi transliterates the received text and adds his own view that the blessing's "maddmad," the doubled word of the Hebrew, is the name Muhammad ﵇ in Hebrew. Bihar also carries a longer narrative in which Abraham is shown the twelve in a vision and told they will come forth "from your firstborn Ishmael." Applied correction: Majlisi says that the reports suggest that “Madmad” is Muhammad's ﷺ name in Hebrew. Bihar also transmits a narrative in which Abraham is told that Muhammad's family will descend from his firstborn, Ishmael.

Known for unverifiable material needs biographical evidence; belongs to dossier is editorial process. Original: The provenance of that vision is weak. Majlisi takes it from Ibn Tawus, who took it from Abu al-Mufaddal al-Shaybani's book of the mutual imprecation, a compiler known for long unverifiable sirah material. It belongs to the dossier as a report, not as evidence of what Abraham saw. Applied correction: Majlisi quotes this narrative from Ibn Tawus's Iqbal al-A'mal. Ibn Tawus names Abu al-Mufaddal al-Shaybani's book on the mutual imprecation and al-Hasan ibn Isma'il ibn Ashnas's work on the observances of Dhu al-Hijja among his sources.

Classified exactly is empty; strongest unexplained; later dozens claim uncited. Preserve natural historical referent and difference from Imami rereading. Original: Classified exactly, this line is a reading of the Torah made by Muslims, resting in its strongest form, al-Nu'mani's, on the dictation of a named Jewish scholar, not on a chain to an Imam. Genesis itself then names the twelve princes as Ishmael's own sons, born in his lifetime (Genesis 25:13-16), and that is the natural historical reading of the promise. The Imami application reads the twelve forward into the nation that came from him instead. After al-Nu'mani and al-Rawandi it becomes a standing argument, carried by al-Hurr al-Amili through al-Bayadi and by later scholars in dozens of volumes. The Bible promises twelve princes from Ishmael. The Islamic corpus counts twelve Imams from Ishmael's greatest descendant. The numerical link is a reasoned reading of Genesis 17:20, and its classical home in the school is the Ghayba of al-Nu'mani. Applied correction: Genesis 25:13–16 identifies twelve princes as Ishmael's sons. Al-Nu'mani's application to the Imams treats the promise as extending to later descendants of Ishmael. He reports a Jewish scholar's dictation transmitted to him through Abd al-Halim ibn al-Husayn al-Samuri; this passage gives no chain to an Imam.

No need to announce independence from Bible or rank frequency. Original: The count does not depend on the Bible. The Imami hadith corpus transmits it, and the Tablet of Fatimah ﵍ is its widest report. Al-Kulayni records it in al-Kafi. Applied correction: Al-Kafi reports that Jabir saw a tablet in Fatimah's hands naming members of her family and their successors.

Copied as fact must be attributed. Preserve names sequence and transmission only once. Original: Jabir copied the tablet, and Imam al-Baqir ﵇ read the copy back letter for letter. Its text names the twelve in order, from Ali ﵇ the trustee through al-Hasan ﵇ and al-Husayn ﵇ to "Mim Ha Mim Dal, a mercy to the worlds," the awaited one. Al-Saduq carries the Tablet in Kamal al-Din and Uyun Akhbar al-Rida, al-Tusi in his Ghayba and his Amali, and al-Khazzaz in al-Kifaya, through chains that differ and converge on Jabir. Applied correction: According to the Tablet report, Jabir copied its text and al-Baqir recited it in agreement with his copy. The text describes a sequence of successors ending with “Mim Ha Mim Dal.” Versions also appear in al-Saduq's Kamal al-Din and Uyun Akhbar al-Rida; al-Hurr al-Amili additionally lists a version in al-Tusi's Ghayba.

Same works listed again after quote; five introduced then four named. Original: Beside the Tablet, the count is stated in plain words and preserved in five cited works, Kamal al-Din, Uyun Akhbar al-Rida, Ithbat al-Hudat, and Bihar al-Anwar among them. Applied correction:

List is useful only if it establishes transmission dependence; preserve that specifically. Original: Kamal al-Din, Uyun Akhbar al-Rida, Ithbat al-Hudat, and Bihar al-Anwar all carry it, and al-Hurr al-Amili notes that al-Khazzaz carried it from Ibn Babawayh with the same chain. Applied correction: Al-Hurr al-Amili notes that al-Khazzaz transmits this report from Ibn Babawayh through the same chain.

Tradition ties and deliberately records add rhetorical weight. Original: The Tradition also ties its twelve to Israel's twelve, in a report whose Sunni chains al-Saduq deliberately records. Applied correction: Al-Saduq cites reports transmitted by Sunni traditionists as support for the Imami count of twelve.

Opponents' own performs a victory. Preserve al-Saduq's attributed reasoning; tribal background needs locus. Original: Saduq's opening report ties the count to the nuqaba, the twelve tribal chiefs Moses appointed, one from each tribe, when the land was first scouted. The opponents' own widespread reports validate the Imami reports about the twelve Imams, as al-Saduq argues, and al-Kafi carries the comparison with the twelve trustees of Isa ﵇. Applied correction: The nuqaba are the twelve chiefs of the Children of Israel. Al-Saduq argues that the Sunni reports corroborate the Imami count of twelve. A report in al-Kafi also compares Muhammad's twelve trustees with the twelve trustees of Jesus.

Completes series in own chapter is empty. Original: The trustees after Muhammad ﷺ run on the pattern of the trustees of Jesus ﵇, and they were twelve. The stranger in the Sacred Mosque who testifies to each Imam by name in sequence, whom Ali ﵇ identifies as al-Khidr, completes the series in al-Kafi's own chapter. Applied correction: Another report in al-Kafi attributes the succession testimony to a visitor whom Ali ﵇ identifies as al-Khidr. He names the first eleven Imams and identifies the twelfth by descent.

Publicly no one adds a claim about recognition absent from the quotation. Original: The last of the twelve is "a man from the descendants of al-Hasan, who is neither given a kunyah nor named until his affair appears, and he will fill it with justice as it has been filled with tyranny." A kunyah is an honorific byname, Abu so-and-so, and the report's point is that the twelfth one is publicly no one at all until he rises. Applied correction: A kunyah is a byname such as Abu so-and-so. The report says that the twelfth is neither named nor called by a kunyah until his affair becomes manifest.

Their own scholars grade highly is unspecific authentication. Original: The Sunni collections carry the number with chains their own scholars grade highly. Sahih Muslim transmits the report of Jabir ibn Samura through a cluster of chains. Applied correction: Sahih Muslim transmits Jabir ibn Samura's report of twelve caliphs from Quraysh through several chains.

Matters most for Bible question announces ranking. Original: The Musnad of Ahmad carries the parallel that matters most for the Bible question, in the report of Masruq. Applied correction: The anthology Ahadith al-Mahdi min Musnad Ahmad ibn Hanbal transmits Ibn Mas'ud's report comparing twelve caliphs with the twelve chiefs of the Children of Israel, citing Musnad Ahmad, vol. 1, p. 398.

Gives reports form says nothing. Keep placement because Mahdi chapter links topics. Original: The Sunan of Abu Dawud devotes a chapter to the Mahdi and gives the reports their form. Applied correction: Abu Dawud includes the following report in his chapter on the Mahdi.

Superlative grading and sole obstacle require evidence. Preserve father-name conflict and attributed al-Kanji judgment, pending corroboration. Original: One clause of this report, "and whose father's name corresponds to my father's name," is absent from Ibn Hanbal's transmissions of the same report, and al-Kanji al-Shafi'i, who collected the Mahdi reports in the seventh century, noted the absence, recorded the harmonizations proposed to keep the clause, and dismissed them as forced. The clause is the one obstacle to reading the report of the twelfth Imam, whose father was al-Hasan ﵇ and not Abdullah, and it is precisely the clause the strongest chains do not carry. Applied correction: Abu Dawud's quoted report includes a clause giving the ruler's father the Prophet's father's name. This does not match the Imami identification of the Mahdi as the son of al-Hasan. Al-Kanji, as quoted in Sharh Ihqaq al-Haqq, discusses attempts to reconcile the clause, calls that interpretation strained, and appeals to Ahmad's transmissions without it (vol. 33, pp. 943–944).
The report immediately following gives exact citation and content. Original: The Sunni commentary tradition itself records the problem. Applied correction:

Tally of rulers already past is loaded. One Sunni voice and past history may misrepresent attributed Ibn Abbas setting. Original: Al-Nawawi records the two objections, the thirty-year caliphate report and the plain fact that more than twelve have ruled, and gives al-Qadi Iyad's answers, that the thirty years are the caliphate of prophethood while the twelve carry no such condition, and that the Prophet said twelve would rule, not that only twelve would rule, so the count was already completed and the later rulers do not harm it. The second answer turns the prophecy into a tally of rulers already past. One Sunni voice in Kanz al-Ummal read the whole set as past history, twelve commanders then the Hour, and was corrected by Ibn Abbas himself, as the entry records, that after the twelve come al-Mansur, al-Saffah, and the Mahdi who hands the affair to Isa ﵇. Applied correction: Al-Nawawi quotes al-Qadi Iyad's distinction between the thirty years of prophetic caliphate and the twelve rulers, for whom no such condition is stated. Al-Qadi also argues that a prediction of twelve rulers permits later rulers. A report in Kanz al-Ummal attributes a related answer to Ibn Abbas: after twelve commanders would come al-Mansur, al-Saffah, and the Mahdi, who would hand authority to Jesus.

Counterevidence of a kind labels without explaining; rulers he knew imputes author/time. Original: That report reads the Mahdi as an Abbasid caliph, and it is counterevidence of a kind. It shows one reader in the Sunni corpus pressing the number onto the rulers he knew. Applied correction:
Treats all passages as one end-time king before explaining why. Original: The Bible's end-time king is described across Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, the Psalms, and Daniel. Applied correction:

None of this is too broad; sentence makes a doctrinal conclusion without specifying literal public fulfillment. Original: None of this occurred in the first century. John's Gospel records the scene before Pilate. Applied correction:

Declines kingdom is not entailed by John18:36. Confirms essential point creates triumphal framing. Christian answer requires named source; nonfulfillment depends on interpretive premises. Original: Jesus ﵇ before Pilate declines an earthly kingdom. The nations did not stream to Zion's law, the swords did not become plowshares, the dispersed were not gathered under one Davidic shepherd, and Rome was not broken and replaced. The standard Christian answer is that the promises await the second coming, and that answer confirms the essential point. They were not fulfilled by the first advent. Applied correction: Before Pilate, Jesus ﵇ says that his kingdom is not from this world and that his servants are not fighting to prevent his surrender. This statement does not exclude a future reign on earth. On a reading that requires worldwide peace and a public reign of justice, the prophetic promises extend beyond the events of Jesus's earthly ministry.

Eliminate claims too much; dispute changes its shape is internal analysis. Needed alternative can be stated directly after primary-source verification. Original: These texts do not logically eliminate the Christian claim that Jesus ﵇ himself returns and performs them. What they eliminate is the claim that they were already fulfilled in the ministry of Jesus of Nazareth. Once the Christian places the fulfillment in the future, the dispute changes its shape. It is no longer whether the prophecies await a future just ruler. It is who that ruler is, and whether the returning Isa ﵇ is himself the king or stands behind another. Applied correction: A future fulfillment could still be attributed to the returning Jesus. Identifying the ruler with the Mahdi requires additional evidence.

Van den Biesen affirms Christ's future return while also describing Augustine's interpretation of the millennium as the Church's present spiritual life. The Christian account he presents therefore includes both present and future fulfillment (Catholic Encyclopedia, “Apocalypse,” 1907, “Purpose of the book”).

Why first advent did not exhaust it presumes every interpretive conclusion. Original: | Passage | What it promises | Why the first advent did not exhaust it | Applied correction: | Passage | What it promises | Implication on a literal public reading |

Christian centuries extends time/claim without evidence. Original: | Isaiah 2:2-4, Micah 4:1-4 | Nations judged by God's law, weapons turned to farm tools, war unlearned | No such public order followed in Palestine or in the Christian centuries | Applied correction: | Isaiah 2:2–4, Micah 4:1–4 | God judges among the nations; weapons become farming tools, and nations cease learning war | Describes public peace among nations |

Replace unexplained global transformation with concrete scope; preserve passage locus formatting when applying. Original: | Isaiah 11:1-9 | A Jesse-rooted ruler judges the poor, slays the wicked, fills the earth with the knowledge of God | The global transformation did not occur | Applied correction: | Isaiah 11:1–9 | A ruler from Jesse's line judges the poor and slays the wicked; the earth is full of the knowledge of God | Describes justice, freedom from harm on the holy mountain, and knowledge of God filling the earth |

Useful comparison is the stated public condition. Original: | Jeremiah 23:5-8, 33:14-16 | A righteous Branch reigns, Judah and Israel dwell securely | No restored, secure Judah and Israel under his rule | Applied correction: | Jeremiah 23:5–8, 33:14–16 | A righteous Branch from David's line executes justice; Judah is saved, Israel dwells safely in chapter 23, and Jerusalem dwells safely in chapter 33 | Describes Davidic rule, security, and Israel's return to its land |

Expose inference from verse rather than announcing failure. Original: | Ezekiel 37:21-28 | One kingdom, one Davidic shepherd, a permanent sanctuary in the midst | Neither the reunification nor the settled sanctuary occurred | Applied correction: | Ezekiel 37:21–28 | Israel is gathered into one nation under David as king and shepherd, with God's sanctuary among them forever | Describes reunification, rule, and a permanent sanctuary |

Reader needs what universal claim means. Original: | Psalm 72 | The king judges the poor, crushes the oppressor, rules to the ends of the earth, peace while the moon endures | The language is worldwide and governmental and was not realized | Applied correction: | Psalm 72 | The king judges the poor, crushes the oppressor, rules to the ends of the earth, and brings peace while the moon endures | Describes justice, abundance, and far-reaching dominion |

Rome requires interpretive argument; not stated in quoted verses. Original: | Daniel 2:44, 7:13-14, 7:27 | God's kingdom crushes and replaces the world kingdoms, all nations serve it | Rome was not crushed or replaced by the mission | Applied correction: | Daniel 2:44, 7:13–14, 7:27 | God establishes an enduring kingdom; one like a son of man receives dominion, and the holy people receive the kingdom | Describes lasting dominion and the displacement of the kingdoms in the vision |

Keep the report's direct claim. Original: Against that job description the Islamic corpus names a candidate, from the Prophet's ﷺ own house, from Fatimah's ﵍ children. Applied correction: Reports in Sunan Abi Dawud describe the Mahdi as a descendant of Fatimah who will fill the earth with justice.

Fullest ranks all reports without support. Original: Ibn al-Munadi's al-Malahim, a Sunni book of the end times, carries the fullest form of the reign. Applied correction: A report in Ibn al-Munadi's al-Malahim describes equal distribution of wealth during the Mahdi's reign.

Empties treasury of petitioners is decorative and may imply literal emptying. Original: The correspondence with the seventy-second psalm's king is functional. That king judges the poor and the needy, breaks the oppressor, and has dominion from sea to sea. Isaiah's ruler judges the poor with righteousness. The Prophet's ﷺ report makes the Mahdi the one who reverses an earth filled with injustice. The Bible's king brings abundance and peace while the moon endures. The Mahdi's reign fills hearts with sufficiency and empties the treasury of petitioners. Applied correction: Psalm 72 describes a king who judges the poor, defeats oppressors, and brings abundance and peace. The Mahdi reports likewise describe justice and material sufficiency. These shared features support a comparison, while the lineage specified in Isaiah and Jeremiah remains a separate difficulty.

Distinction matters and reports draw themselves add nothing; another as imam needs source adjudication. Original: The distinction that matters is the one the reports draw themselves. The returning Isa ﵇ is present, and another is the imam. Applied correction:

Preserve essential source distinction. Original: The report does not name the imam. The Shia corpus names him, in reports that fuse the count, the lineage, and the prayer behind him. Applied correction: Ahmad's report leaves the imam unnamed. The following Imami report identifies the Mahdi as the last of twelve successors and says that Jesus will pray behind him.

Replays nearly every clause of translation. Original: Twelve successors, the first Ali ﵇, the last the Mahdi, and then Isa ﵇ son of Mary, the Spirit of God, descends and prays behind him, and the earth shines with the light of its Lord, and his authority reaches east and west. Imam al-Rida ﵇ states it in al-Ma'mun's own assembly. Applied correction: Uyun Akhbar al-Rida attributes the same prediction of Jesus praying behind the Mahdi to al-Rida in a discussion with al-Ma'mun.
Callout identifies Gabriel and source; no unique claim. Original: Al-Kafi carries it in Gabriel's words to the Prophet ﷺ. Applied correction:

Every one of us adopts quoted speaker's voice. Original: Every one of us bears allegiance to the tyrant of his age on his neck, except the Qa'im, behind whom Isa ﵇ son of Mary will pray. God hides his birth and conceals his person so that no allegiance binds him when he rises. Applied correction: In the report attributed to al-Hasan, God conceals the Qa'im's birth so that he will owe no allegiance to the ruler of his time when he emerges.

Prayer leadership does not itself transfer biblical Davidic kingship to Mahdi. Must preserve objection rather than narrate it away. Original: The Davidic lineage of these kings needs its own word, because the Prophet's ﷺ house is not David's line. The framework already distinguishes the returning Isa ﵇, the son of David, who confirms the truth, from the divinely guided ruler of the final order, and it places the Davidic king inside the Mahdi's kingdom rather than on its throne. A Christian who insists the Davidic king must himself reign has the reports of both traditions to weigh, which give the throne to a man from the Prophet's ﷺ house while Isa ﵇ stands behind him in prayer. The Bible's king who reigns, judges, fights, and fills the earth with justice needs a reign, a judgment, a war, and a transformation. The Gospels record that Isa קּ declined the kingdom before Pilate. Applied correction: Isaiah 11 describes a ruler from Jesse's line, and Jeremiah 23 names David's line. The Mahdi reports quoted here identify him through Muhammad's ﷺ and Fatimah's ﵍ line. The Imami prediction that Jesus ﵇ will pray behind the Mahdi distinguishes the two figures, but it does not identify the Mahdi as David's descendant or explicitly assign him every office described in these biblical passages. The comparison remains functional; the difference in lineage is unresolved.
Case establishes frames method rather than subject. Original: ## What the case establishes and what it does not Applied correction:

Sources already cited beside their claims; this card is not evidence. Original: - **Source:** Christian holders. Pius XII, Munificentissimus Deus 27 (1950) for the Marian reading; Catholic Encyclopedia, "Apocalypse" (1907) for the Church and Israel readings and the Genesis 37 background; Ilzam al-Nasib, vol. 1, p. 130, for the church reading known to Muslim polemic Applied correction:
No new locator. Original: - **Source:** Islamic exhibits quoted above, Shia and Sunni, cited in their sections Applied correction:
No claim expressed beyond topic names. Original: - **Claim:** the compared offices, woman, twelve, and reigning king, and who fills them Applied correction:

Three readings counts wrong or ambiguous (three woman readings plus Muslim). All rest covered previously. Original: Three readings now stand side by side. The Christian readings assign the woman to Mary, to the Church, or to Israel, and assign the reigning king to a future advent of Jesus ﵇. The reading documented above assigns the woman's sun, moon, and twelve stars to the figures the Islamic corpus itself names, the twelve princes of Ishmael to the twelve Imams ﵈, and the reigning king to the Mahdi with Isa ﵇ behind him. Applied correction:

On textual fidelity and each step labeled describes editorial work; church-authority reduction needs source evidence. Original: On textual fidelity, the comparison runs this way. The Islamic corpus transmits each element, the sun as the Prophet ﷺ and the moon as Ali ﵇ in the exegesis of Qur'an 91, the nine shining stars as the Imams from al-Husayn's line in the Salman report, the count of twelve in the Tablet and its family of reports, and the justice-filling ruler from Fatimah's ﵍ line. The connection of those fixed elements to the Bible's sign is a modern inference, and each step above has been labeled where inference begins. The Christian readings of the same sign are also assignments, older and internally divided, resting on the authority the reader grants the church. Neither side can prove its assignment from the text alone, because the text names no one. Applied correction:

Narrower firmer praises result; Christian must answer suppresses interpretive alternatives. Original: What the case establishes is narrower and firmer. If the promised Messiah has already come and completed his messianic work, where are the outcomes the prophets promised, the universal law, the peace among nations, the destroyed oppressor kingdoms, the gathered and secure Israel, the worldwide justice? A Christian must answer that they remain future. The question left standing is who fills those offices. The Sunni strand of the reports leaves him unnamed at the descent, and the Imami strand names his line from the children of Fatimah. The Islamic corpus is the one that names him. Applied correction:

Repeats whole article; exactly that number conceals contested identification; both traditions conflate named and unnamed imam; each step marked leaks review process. Original: > The woman of Revelation 12 is a sign of a sun, a moon, and twelve stars around one woman. The Qur'an swears by the sun and the moon, and the Imams named them the Prophet ﷺ and Ali ﵇. Both schools count twelve from Quraysh, and the Imami reports name all twelve, first Ali קּ and last the Mahdi, eleven of them Fatimah's כֿ descendants. Genesis promises twelve princes from Ishmael, and the line of Ishmael's greatest descendant carried exactly that number of guides. The prophets promise a reigning king of worldwide justice, and the reports of both traditions describe him from the Prophet's ﷺ progeny, with Isa ﵇ returned and praying behind him. The Bible supplies the job description. The Islamic corpus supplies the names. The connection between them is a reading, and each step has been marked where inference begins. Applied correction: > These biblical passages and Imami reports share celestial imagery, a count of twelve, and descriptions of just rule. Applying the biblical figures to Fatimah ﵍, the Imams, and the Mahdi remains an interpretation: the twelve-star crown differs from the Islamic reports' distribution of symbols, Genesis identifies Ishmael's twelve princes as his sons, and Isaiah and Jeremiah specify Jesse's or David's line. The quoted Imami reports expressly describe Jesus ﵇ praying behind the Mahdi or Qa'im. The report attributed to Ahmad leaves the imam unnamed.
